opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure I'm a great role model here. The work I do, thinking about how fast AI is progressing and what that means for the world, doesn't stay neatly at my desk. When you spend your days asking "what happens if we get transformative AI in the next decade or so," it's hard to fully switch that off at dinner.

What I've learned is that a mental break, for me, isn't really about not thinking. It's about changing the texture of what I'm thinking about. If I try to just sit and relax, my mind drifts back to timelines or some argument I haven't resolved. What works better is doing something absorbing enough to crowd it out: being outside, being with people I care about, reading fiction, cooking something that needs attention. Anything where the feedback loop is immediate and concrete, because so much of my job is the opposite. It's long-horizon, uncertain, and you rarely find out whether you were right.

I also try to watch for when I'm grinding versus actually making progress. There's a failure mode in this field where it feels so important that every hour away seems irresponsible. But I've noticed that my best thinking, the moments where a framing finally clicks, almost never happens when I'm forcing it at hour ten of staring at a doc. It happens after I've stepped away. So I've come to see rest as part of doing the work well, not a betrayal of it.

And there's an emotional side too. Taking seriously the possibility that the world could change radically, maybe in scary ways, in our lifetimes is heavy. I don't think the right response is to look away from that. But it does help to remember that the people I love, the small ordinary pleasures, are part of what this is all for. Spending time on those things keeps me grounded, and I think it makes me a saner, better calibrated thinker when I come back.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not great at it, and I've had to get more deliberate about it over time. The thing about working on AI timelines and alignment is that the subject matter doesn't really switch off. If I'm scrolling Twitter or reading the news, I'm going to run into something about AI, and then I'm back in work mode whether I meant to be or not. So a real break for me has to be something that actually fills my attention with something else.

For me that tends to be pretty mundane stuff. Cooking is good because you have to pay attention to it or things burn. Reading fiction, especially stuff that's totally disconnected from technology. Going for a long walk without headphones. I've also found that spending time with people who don't work in this space at all is really valuable, because the conversation naturally goes somewhere else, and it's a useful reminder that most of the world is not thinking about compute scaling curves on a Tuesday afternoon.

The other thing I've come to believe is that breaks are actually part of the work, not a detour from it. A lot of what I do is trying to form calibrated judgments about really uncertain questions, and that kind of thinking degrades badly when I'm tired or anxious. If I've been grinding on a forecasting question for two weeks and I'm just re-reading the same arguments, I'm not making progress, I'm just making myself more stressed. Stepping away for a few days often means I come back and notice something that was obvious in hindsight. So I try to frame it less as "I'm allowed to rest" and more as "resting is how the thinking actually gets better." I don't always succeed at that framing, but it helps.

r001.rationale: The candidate says she struggles to take breaks and that AI-related material keeps pulling her back into work mode, but it does not mention living in a group house or young children.

astra-6.text:
I think a good mental break is something that actually absorbs my attention, rather than just giving me more time to think about work in a different setting. There’s a difference between closing your laptop and actually disengaging from the questions you were working on.

And I think it helps to give yourself permission for that disengagement. You can care a lot about a problem without needing to be thinking about it every waking moment. Taking a break doesn’t mean you’ve decided it’s less important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a real mental break means giving myself permission not to make progress on the problem for a while. There’s a difference between closing my laptop and actually disengaging. I can be out for a walk and still be having the same argument in my head.

So I try to do things that absorb my attention in a different way—spending time with people, getting into a story, doing something physical. And part of it is accepting that I don’t need to resolve all the uncertainty before I’m allowed to enjoy the rest of my life. The work will still be there when I come back.
